paragraphs.heading: Two craft, three agencies
paragraphs.text: Cassini–Huygens, usually just called Cassini, was a mission to study Saturn along with its rings and moons. Three space agencies shared the work: NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), and Italy's space agency (ASI). It had two parts: the Cassini orbiter and ESA's Huygens probe, which landed on Titan, Saturn's largest moon. The orbiter was named for Giovanni Domenico Cassini, who discovered divisions in Saturn's rings and four of its moons. The probe was named for Christiaan Huygens, who discovered Titan.

paragraphs.heading: The long road to Saturn
paragraphs.text: Cassini launched on October 15, 1997, on a Titan IV-B rocket. The trip took almost seven years and passed Venus twice, Earth once, the asteroid 2685 Masursky and Jupiter along the way. On July 1, 2004 it entered orbit around Saturn. It was the fourth probe to visit Saturn, but the first to go into orbit there.

paragraphs.heading: Landing on Titan
paragraphs.text: Huygens rode along with Cassini until the two separated on December 25, 2004. On January 14, 2005, Huygens came down on Titan by parachute. It sent back data for about 90 minutes, using the orbiter to relay it to Earth. This was the first landing anywhere in the outer Solar System, and the first on any moon other than our own.

paragraphs.heading: A mission that kept going
paragraphs.text: The original plan was four years of work at Saturn, from June 2004 to May 2008. The mission was then extended twice: first to September 2010 as the Cassini Equinox Mission, then for seven more years as the Cassini Solstice Mission. NASA's planetary science director, Jim Green, called it a "mission of firsts". In his words, it transformed our picture of Saturn's moons and rings and of the places in the Solar System where life could exist.

paragraphs.heading: The Grand Finale
paragraphs.text: In its last phase, called the Grand Finale, Cassini threaded the gaps between Saturn and its inner rings several times, a risky set of passes. The goal was to squeeze out as much science as possible before the end. On September 15, 2017, it was sent into Saturn's upper atmosphere, where it burned up. This was done on purpose to protect Saturn's moons, some of which might offer habitable places. A spacecraft that could no longer be steered might have crashed into one and carried stowaway microbes from Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Who built it and what it cost
paragraphs.text: People from 27 countries designed, built, flew and gathered data from the two craft. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory developed the orbiter and managed the mission, and the European Space Research and Technology Centre developed Huygens. The whole mission cost about US$3.26 billion. The United States paid about 80 percent, ESA about 15 percent and ASI about 5 percent, according to a press kit prepared in October 2000.
